What kind of color this is

True Blue occupies a specific position in the blue range: saturated, primary-adjacent, and unambiguous once you land on it. The hex breakdown tells the story quickly — 01 red, FC green, CC blue. That red value of 01 means there's essentially no warm component bleeding into the shade. Green sits at 252 in decimal, which is substantial, but combined with the maximum blue value, the result still reads as distinctly blue rather than cyan.

This matters because players sometimes confuse True Blue with lighter sky blues or deeper navy variants. The distinction comes down to saturation and lightness. At #010FCC, you're looking at a medium-to-high lightness blue with strong saturation. It isn't pastel, and it isn't dark enough to be mistaken for midnight tones. Think standard blue printer ink, not royal navy.

Start by establishing whether you're in the right hue family. A guess like Teal (#008080) or Purple (#800080) eliminates large swaths of possibility but doesn't get you close to this answer specifically. Better opening moves target adjacent blues: Cornflower (#6C91C5 from July 1st), Cerulean variations, or even a basic medium blue like #4169E1.

From there, the saturation clues guide you. If your guess returns a high saturation reading but the hue leans too light or too dark, adjust accordingly. Going slightly darker than #010FCC might look like Navy (#000080), while stepping lighter could push into powder blue territory. The sweet spot is medium-lightness with that maximum blue channel holding strong.

Recent history gives useful calibration. July 4th's Airforce was desaturated and darker. July 3rd's Soft Pink is irrelevant to today's puzzle but reminds you that the rotation doesn't follow predictable lightness patterns. Use those anchor points to reset your mental baseline before guessing.

Where players usually go wrong

The most common error with shades like True Blue is overthinking the saturation. Some players assume "True" implies maximum saturation across all channels, which would point toward cyan or a more electric blue. That's not how this particular naming convention works. True Blue describes the purity of the hue within the blue family, not its brightness relative to other colors entirely.

Another pitfall involves confusing this with Royal Blue (#4169E1). Royal Blue sits noticeably lighter and carries a slight purple undertone. If your guesses cluster around that area without success, drift darker and purer — away from the violet edge of blue.

Players also stumble when they fixate on the date number. Day 1563 has no relationship to the color. Treat it as metadata, not a clue.

How the score logic actually helps

The scoring system in Colordle measures three things: hue proximity, saturation difference, and lightness delta. For a color like True Blue, the hue score rewards anything in the blue family strongly. Saturation scores become critical when distinguishing between similar blues — a pale sky blue will register lower saturation than #010FCC, signaling you're off-target even if the hue reading looks promising.

Lightness scoring completes the picture. Medium-lightness colors like True Blue sit between pastel and shadow. If your guess returns a lightness score far from center, you're either too bright or too dark. The combination of these three readings lets you triangulate without burning excessive guesses on wild swings.

In practice, that means checking all three indicators after each guess rather than focusing solely on hue match. A perfect hue score with poor saturation and lightness readings tells you the family is right but the specific shade needs adjustment in two dimensions simultaneously.

Colorfle answer today: how the mix should be read

What the source colors are telling you

Each color in the source palette carries information about the solve path. Bright saturated sources tend to appear when the target leans toward primary or secondary hues. Muted or pastel sources suggest the target sits closer to gray or has balanced channel values.

Look at the hint widget if one exists on today's page. Some versions of Colorfle include a "closest match" indicator that flags which of your three guesses is nearest to the target. That single data point can save multiple failed submissions by narrowing your search to the two weaker matches.

The solver link available on this site lets you input your current best guesses and receive feedback on channel-by-channel distance. Using that tool systematically beats random tweaking because it quantifies your errors instead of relying on eyeballing.

Why additive color logic beats random mixing

Additive color mixing follows predictable math. Red (255, 0, 0) plus Green (0, 255, 0) equals Yellow (255, 255, 0). Adding Blue (0, 0, 255) gets you to White (255, 255, 255). This isn't intuitive if you learned color theory through art class, where red plus green makes brown.

The mental shift matters. Think in terms of adding light channels together rather than blending physical pigments. When you see a target color like teal (0, 128, 128), your brain might instinctively reach for blue-green paint mixing. But digitally, teal is simply half-intensity green combined with half-intensity blue, with red set to zero.

A careful player usually notices that targets with high saturation require source colors near the corners of the RGB cube—pure or near-pure primaries and secondaries. Desaturated targets demand lower values across all three channels or careful balance toward neutral gray.

Easy adjustment path for the next Colorfle

Before guessing randomly, map out the RGB cube mentally. Identify which corner of the color space your target occupies. Then work backward to determine which three sources could converge there.

If you're consistently missing by a small margin on one channel, check whether you've been underestimating how much that channel contributes to the final mix. Sometimes a color looks predominantly blue but actually contains significant green—the eye plays tricks, but the numbers don't lie.

The archive history linked from this page offers pattern recognition over multiple puzzles. Reviewing past solutions builds intuition for how often certain channel combinations appear and which color families prove trickiest.

Does the order of my three colors matter?

No. The game mixes all three sources simultaneously regardless of sequence. What matters is getting each individual channel value close enough to the target that the combined result matches within the acceptable tolerance.

What if my hints show zero progress on one color?

Zero progress typically means that particular source is completely wrong—not just slightly off. Revisit your assumption about that channel's contribution to the target. Gray targets require low values across all three channels with minimal variation between them. Your three sources should cluster near (128, 128, 128) or whatever gray level the target specifies. Any single channel that spikes above the others will drag the mix toward that hue.

Players often misinterpret the heat scale. "Warm" doesn't mean adjacent—it means you're in the same hemisphere rough zone, usually within 2,000 kilometers. "Hot" means closer, typically under 1,000 kilometers. Cold means you're looking at the wrong continent entirely.

A single large territory gives you almost no directional signal compared to a smaller country with a clear neighbor set.

Another common mistake: players assume symmetry in the heat system. They think "warm" always means roughly the same distance threshold regardless of direction. It doesn't. Latitude matters. A country two zones north of yours reads differently than one two zones east, even at similar distances. The algorithm weights proximity along both axes.

If you've been stuck for several rounds, check the archive link for past puzzles with similar heat patterns. The underlying logic hasn't changed—today's mystery country follows the same rules as every other day's solution.

Think in triangles, not lines. One guess narrows nothing. Two guesses give you a line. Three guesses give you a triangle, and where those three lines overlap tells you far more than any single reading.

Pick three anchor countries that form a rough triangle around your target region. For example, if you suspect Central America, guess Mexico, Colombia, and Venezuela. The heat readings from all three create an intersection zone. Whatever falls inside that intersection is your real candidate area.

This method works especially well for islands and coastal nations that sit between larger continental landmasses. Players who skip triangulation end up guessing Jamaica, then Puerto Rico, then Cuba—three separate mistakes—when they could have identified the Caribbean basin in two tries using Panama and Venezuela as anchors.

When simple words do more than precise ones

A guess like "tree" will almost always outperform "arboreal" unless the secret word specifically calls for precision. Same with "water" over "aquatic" or "running" over "ambulatory." You're not writing poetry here; you're speaking the language the model learned.

If everything scores in the 20s, you're probably too narrow. Swing wide. It means words that appear in similar contexts across training data tend to score higher together. "Coffee" and "morning" score well because they co-occur frequently. "Coffee" and "geology" score poorly despite both being nouns. The model learned associations, not definitions.
